summary: A 1975 note on a change to the protocol between IMPs and hosts. It replaces RFC 687.

eli5.summary: This note finalises a change to how computers and network routers talk, replacing an earlier proposal.

questions: how did arpanet support more than 63 imps
subtitle: A 1975 plan to widen the IMP-to-host protocol so the ARPANET could address hosts on more than 63 IMPs.

tldr.problem: The IMP/host protocol limited the network to 63 IMPs, and there were already 62.
tldr.mechanism: The leader grows from two to six 16-bit words, the address field grows to 32 bits, and new fields and message handling options are added while old and new formats run side by side.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 687 and keeps the protocol backwards compatible, so hosts can switch over gradually.

today: This RFC revises RFC 687. Its status is listed as Unknown, and the text only sketches the plan and promises a draft of changes to Report 1822.

sections.title: Why the Protocol Is Changing
sections.content:
This note revises RFC 687 and sketches an expansion of the IMP/host and host/IMP protocol. Among other things it allows addressing hosts on more than 63 IMPs, since there were already 62 IMPs.

BBN does not attempt fundamental changes to the protocol philosophy, because it cannot make massive changes on the short time scale of current needs. A knowledge of Section 3 of BBN Report 1822 is assumed.
sections.eli5: The network was nearly full, so they stretch the old rules a bit rather than inventing new ones.

sections.title: Bigger Leader and Address Fields
sections.content:
The leader grows from two to six 16-bit words, which is 96 bits instead of 32. That causes word-boundary trouble for some hosts. With a total leader of 136 bits, only machines with 8-, 16-, 32- and 64-bit words fit well. So a host may tell its IMP a number of 16-bit padding words to insert between the leaders. For instance, 24-bit machines can ask for one word and 10- and 36-bit machines for five.

The address field grows to 32 bits, with 16 bits of IMP address and 8 bits for a future network address. A new 16-bit message length field lets the source host optionally tell the network the message length in bits. The maximum packets per message rises to 16 from 8, and the handling type field expands to eight bits.
sections.eli5: The message label gets bigger to hold longer addresses, and a host that likes a different size can ask for padding to line things up.

sections.title: New Handling and Interface Features
sections.content:
Several features are added. A source host can choose how many packets a multi-packet message uses, such as two or five, which may give better service. Unordered (type-3) messages become a subtype of type 0, which is slightly incompatible for the three or so hosts that use them. The For/From IMP bit goes away, and fake host addresses become the four highest host numbers, so the IMP Teletype is host 252. The IMP to host NOP gains a parameter with the host's address.

A mechanism will also let the IMP refuse a message without blocking the host interface, then ask the host to resend it. The maximum data in a single-packet message may drop by a few bits. The packets-per-message and non-blocking features come after the basic changes.
sections.eli5: Hosts get more control over how their messages travel, and the network can say wait a moment without freezing the host.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Old and new formats are supported in parallel in the IMPs for the foreseeable future. A host picks the mode through the format of its host to IMP NOP message, and may switch back and forth for debugging. The IMP starts by sending several NOP messages of each type so the host can choose.

A host that does not use the new format cannot address hosts on IMPs numbered above 63. Where possible the IMPs convert between formats so old-format and new-format hosts can still talk. BBN is drafting the necessary changes to Report 1822.
sections.eli5: Old and new styles work at the same time, so each computer can upgrade whenever it is ready.

references.text: IMP/Host and Host/IMP Protocol Change, RFC 687.
